column4: This event covered SR 504 with rock, mud, ice and water and damaged the Spirit Lake Outlet Bridge at milepost 49, which provided access to the Johnston Ridge Observatory at Mount St Helens (WSDOT, 2024).

WSDOT (Fiske and others, 2023) estimated volume of the source to be about 307,000 cubic yards (~235,000 cubic meters) by differencing lidar they contracted that was flown on 26 May 2023 with pre-event lidar from 2022. This number is only slightly higher than the estimate by Mosbrucker (2025) used as the best estimate of Volume. The WSDOT value is taken as the Volume_high estimate because it was computed using post-event elevation data collected later after the event when additional material could have failed.
Photographs of the source area and deposit, provided by WSDOT, can be seen here: https://www.flickr.com/photos/wsdot/albums/72177720308336123/.
Twelve people and a dog were evacuated by helicopter the following day - Quote from Petely (2023c).

The debris slide originated in deposits from the 18 May 1980 debris avalanche (Eid 6) that spilled over Johnston Ridge and down the other side into this valley. WSDOT (Fiske and others, 2023) notes that these deposits are about 70 m thick in the location of the source area and are underlain by Oligocene aged tuff, basalt, andesite, dacite, and rhyolite bedrock. Field reconnaissance on 22 May 2023 found that there was bedrock exposed along the floor and west side of the source area, and irregular bedrock exposures on the floor of the source area. Source material classified as loose silty sand with gravel to poorly graded sand. Non-plastic.

Volume and Area_source from Mosbrucker (2025). Mosbrucker (2025) estimated the volume of the source to be 234,000 cubic meters, maximum elevation change of 73 m, and the area of the source to be 20,700 m2. These estimates were based on differencing pre-event lidar collected in 2022 and post-event point cloud derived from structure-from-motion processing of helicopter photos collected on 5/18/2023.

WSDOT analysis and modeling (Fiske and others, 2023) suggested that the landslide was caused by elevated pore water pressures in the material following rapid snow melt during an unseasonably warm period preceding the event. They hypothesize that the event likely started with a flow-like failure at the base of the source area that retrogressed upslope until the deposit drained sufficiently to stabilize.

WSDOT (Fiske and others, 2023) conducted field and UAV reconnaissance and took photos and video the morning after the event and May 22. Collected soil samples of depletion zone. Contracted lidar, flown on 26 May 2023. Conducted limit equilibrium backanalysis of slope stability.

Springs were noted coming from high on the sidewalls immediately after the event. A week after the event those had dried up but springs persisted near the bottom of the sidewall by 22 May 2023. WSDOT concluded this meant groundwater levels were lowered by as much as 50-60 feet by 22 May relative to 15 May.

Maxar, Planet, Google Earth (AirBus), and Sentinel-2 imagery used to make outlines, centerlines, and measure H, L, areas not reported by other sources. NDVI differencing computed from Sentinel-2 imagery comparing before (5/12/23) and after (5/17/23) the event was used to determine the outline of the debris flow.
Volume estimates account only for the source area of the initial debris slide and do not estimate any potential entrainment that may have occurred during the debris flow.

WSDOT (Fiske and others, 2023) reported that the USGS stream gauge (site id 14240311) at outlet of Spirit Lake tunnel, just downstream from the Spirit Lake Outlet bridge stopped recording after 9 pm PDT (4 UTC) when gauge was damaged by the debris flow. Gauge location 46.2822222, -122.1952778 .

High frequency (1-5 Hz) ground velocity waveforms from closest stations with detections. Dashed lines show approximate start and end times of event (from database). Waveforms are corrected for station response after removing the mean. Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present. Clipped waveforms have not been removed before station correction so check raw plots before interpreting high amplitude signals.

Multitaper spectra (same units as Power Spectral Density) of velocity waveforms corrected for station sensitivity from closest stations with detections. Linear trend was removed and a taper was applied before generating spectra. Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present. Since station response was not removed to avoid adding artifacts at low frequencies for short and intermediate period stations, the lower frequency amplitudes should be interpreted with care.
